storyTitle: Show HN: Airtable, a real-time spreadsheet-database hybrid
outcome: Airtable raised $735M at an $11B valuation and became a standard no-code database.
outcomeDetail: Airtable launched publicly in 2014 and grew into a collaboration platform used by hundreds of thousands of teams. By its 2021 Series F it was valued at $11 billion, and it remains an independent company.
note: The critic could not see the gap between Google Apps and a purpose-built relational tool, but that gap turned out to be a large market.

author: titus22
cardQuote: If that's the target audience, then I see Airtable failing also. Surely 80% of the benefit of an excel spreadsheet, or google sheets, for a common user is how bare bones and simple to navigate the two products are?
quote:
If that's the target audience, then I see Airtable failing also. Surely 80% of the benefit of an excel spreadsheet, or google sheets, for a common user is how bare bones and simple to navigate the two products are?

"Oh hey, I just need to fire off some data rapidly in an organized way. Boop, done." And that's the trick, isn't it? The need to rapidly organize previously un-organized data. It's not a case of, "I know exactly how I want to rapidly organize some data."

With Airtable, it would be "I now have to navigate this decoupled spread out GUI and learn what all these abstract terms mean, when all I want to do is calculate how much we spent on ice cream last month."

In essence, it is making the workflow slower for those types of people.

On the other end of the spectrum, from a programmer's point of view, GUI's ALWAYS slow things down. This is why programmers who used VIM / Emacs were faster than those using modern IDE's. It's why hot-keys are important to both technical and non-technical workers. Presentation does not equal productivity. The presentation is what Airtable is pushing as the abstraction for non-technical users.

If the target audience for Airtable is instead small-business startups - then those startups are going to be in for a world of hurt when they need to get into real business development. They will have wasted time, energy, and resources to get set up on a lego platform that they'll need to migrate away from.

Looking at the pricing model and data limitations, there's nothing that would make this a better choice than just hooking up to AWS or something similar, directly. Using Airtable would require maintaining some form of middleware for SPA's...and there's no way in the world that you wouldn't be hitting their caps rapidly. Just an extra cost.

I'm not saying this product won't work well for a market niche, but that niche is a lot smaller than the buzz words thrown around in today's publications.
storyTitle: Airtable gets $52M in funding
outcome: Airtable reached an $11B valuation and kept growing well past the scale the critic thought it could not reach.
outcomeDetail: Airtable raised $52 million in 2018 and then $735 million at an $11 billion valuation in 2021. It remains a widely used tool for teams that want spreadsheet-like data with database structure.
note: The "lego platform" prediction underestimated how much non-technical teams wanted structured views and automations without a developer.

storyTitle: Coda, a “next-generation spreadsheet” – from rows and columns to custom apps
outcome: Coda was valued at $1.4B in 2021 and acquired by Grammarly in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Coda carved out a niche with documents that mix text, tables, and formulas, and raised at a $1.4 billion valuation. Grammarly bought the company in December 2024 and installed Coda co-founder Shishir Mehrotra as CEO.
note: Coda never matched Excel's feature set, but it did not need to; its document-first workflow attracted teams that wanted apps inside docs.

storyTitle: Coda, a “next-generation spreadsheet” – from rows and columns to custom apps
outcome: Coda succeeded without replicating all of Excel, reaching a $1.4B valuation and a Grammarly acquisition.
outcomeDetail: Coda positioned itself as a new document format rather than an Excel replacement and built a base of product and operations teams. Its 2021 Series D valued it at $1.4 billion, and Grammarly acquired it in 2024.
note: The critic assumed switching required feature parity; Coda won users by being different, not by checking every Excel box.

author: jasoncrawford
cardQuote: It turns out that not having to name things is a feature . Users often avoid naming things and dislike being forced to do so.
quote:
It turns out that not having to name things is a feature . Users often avoid naming things and dislike being forced to do so.

The reason is what developers already know: naming things is hard! (Two hard problems, etc.)

Of course, developers also know how valuable good names are, so we like to take the time to pick good names. Users would rather just skip naming altogether and refer to things by letter/number or just by clicking on them.
storyTitle: Coda, a “next-generation spreadsheet” – from rows and columns to custom apps
outcome: Coda's named-object model did not scare users away; the company reached a $1.4B valuation and was acquired in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Coda made named rows, columns, and formulas central to its product and marketed it as a friendlier way to build small apps. It raised at a $1.4 billion valuation in 2021 before Grammarly acquired it.
note: The critique of forced naming was reasonable, but Coda's templates and AI features reduced the burden enough for teams to adopt it.

storyTitle: Joel Spolsky Launches Trello - Organize Anything Together
outcome: Atlassian bought Trello for $425M in 2017, and it reached 50 million users by 2019.
outcomeDetail: Trello spun out of Fog Creek in 2014 and was acquired by Atlassian in January 2017 for $425 million. Atlassian reported 35 million users in March 2019 and 50 million by October 2019.
note: The "who asked for this" dismissal missed that a simple, horizontal kanban board would appeal far beyond software teams.

author: icefox
cardQuote: So I honestly don't get it. Is this a poor mans bug tracker? A possible re-invention of a bug tracker?
quote:
So I honestly don't get it. Is this a poor mans bug tracker? A possible re-invention of a bug tracker? (something wacky and different version of a bug tracker to see if it sticks?)

I have seen people mention project management a bunch, but the view really isn't about viewing what people are doing. In fact items that don't have people assigned to them still show up. The 10 foot view isn't even that good as they all squares and text. At a glance you can not tell what changed recently, what is late etc.

I had to really grimace when it showed the internal team that was using it and one of the stacks was "bugs" and it had the most number of items and was scrollable. ugg Does that scale to thousands of open bugs (or how about just 50)?

So either this is for all of those people who have never discovered the overview page of their bug tracker or maybe it is trying an experiment to see if the process of creating a bug tracker for a project is too difficult and here you just click "new project" and blam done and later on you export it to a real bug tracker... Maybe this is all just tricking users into using a bug tracker without them knowing?

Anyone get the same feeling?
storyTitle: Joel Spolsky Launches Trello - Organize Anything Together
outcome: Trello became a mass-market collaboration tool with 50M users and a $425M Atlassian acquisition.
outcomeDetail: Trello's card-and-list model spread from engineering teams to marketing, sales, and personal planning. Atlassian bought it in 2017 and continued to grow it to tens of millions of users.
note: The critic judged Trello as a bug tracker and found it lacking; users instead treated it as a general-purpose board.

storyTitle: Superhuman is what Gmail would be if built today
outcome: Superhuman built a premium email business and was acquired by Grammarly in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Superhuman charged a premium subscription and built a loyal base of power users despite competing with free Gmail. Grammarly acquired it in July 2025; Superhuman's last private valuation was $825 million, and Grammarly later rebranded its parent company as Superhuman.
note: The "small niche" was real, but it was lucrative: Superhuman built a business valuable enough for Grammarly to buy.

storyTitle: Superhuman is what Gmail would be if built today

outcomeDetail: Superhuman grew a subscription business around speed, keyboard shortcuts, and inbox triage. Grammarly bought it in 2025 and made it part of its AI productivity suite.

storyTitle: Show HN: Obsidian – A knowledge base that works on local Markdown files
outcome: Obsidian stayed closed source but grew to an estimated 1.5 million monthly users and a profitable, user-supported business.
outcomeDetail: Obsidian kept its app proprietary while storing notes as local Markdown files, which blunted lock-in concerns. It remained bootstrapped and user-supported, with press estimates of about 1.5 million monthly active users and roughly $25 million in annual revenue.
note: The open-source objection was principled, but local files gave users most of the exit protection they wanted, and Obsidian thrived without opening its code.

storyTitle: Show HN: Obsidian – A knowledge base that works on local Markdown files
outcome: Obsidian kept personal use free and built a business on optional sync, publish, and commercial licenses.
outcomeDetail: Years after launch, Obsidian still offers free personal use and sells paid sync, publish, and commercial licenses. The company remains independent and says it is 100% supported by its users rather than investors.
note: The skepticism about permanence was understandable, but Obsidian's paid add-ons, not a license change, turned out to be the business model.

author: bryanh
cardQuote: In between are tools that no-one really wants. Basically, don't stop at the editor. Its a feature.
quote:
First of all: congrats on launching! 7 months is a long time, it has to feel good!

A long time ago I built "squeeze page" manager which had an editor like this (it was simpler and more focused on content management). I sunk a lot of time into it. However, I ran into the same problem I bet you guys will run into: "the design tool chasm". On one end are simple tools for publishing on the web (Weebly and Wordpress) and on the other are professional tools (Photoshop and Sublime Text 2/Textmate). In between are tools that no-one really wants.

Basically, don't stop at the editor. Its a feature. Take a look at Unbounce or HubSpot for "marketing tool" inspiration and Weebly and Wordpress for "publishing tool" inspiration. Or, if you want to be used by professional designers, you'll need to go in a whole different direction (which is likely the one you are on now). Of course, if you have target customers that love this as is, their feedback vastly trumps mine. But never stop talking to your target customers (steal them from the big boys with your personal touch and solve their problems)! Good luck guys!
storyTitle: Show HN: Webflow - Design responsive websites visually
outcome: Webflow became a professional no-code web platform valued at $4B in 2022.
outcomeDetail: Webflow raised a $120 million Series C at a $4 billion valuation in March 2022 and was nearing $100 million in annual recurring revenue. It remains a major platform for professional web design.
note: The "design tool chasm" warning was smart, but Webflow crossed it by adding hosting, a CMS, and enough control for professional designers.

storyTitle: Launch HN: Glide (YC W19) – Mobile Apps from Google Sheets

storyTitle: Launch HN: Raycast (YC W20) – CLI-inspired desktop app for non-coding tasks
outcome: Raycast built a large individual-user base, raised a $30M Series B, and expanded toward Windows and iOS.
outcomeDetail: Raycast launched a store of community-built extensions and grew to hundreds of thousands of daily active users. It raised a $30 million Series B in 2024 and began expanding beyond macOS.
note: The critic was right that enterprise selling is hard, but Raycast's bottom-up adoption among developers gave it a business before it needed enterprise contracts.

storyTitle: Fantastical: A new calendar app for Mac launches
outcome: Fantastical became a leading Mac calendar app; Fantastical 2 won a 2015 Apple Design Award.
outcomeDetail: Flexibits kept building on the menu-bar quick-entry idea, adding a full calendar window, natural-language parsing, and iOS apps. Fantastical 2 won an Apple Design Award in 2015, and Flexibits still ships Fantastical across Apple platforms.
note: The 1.0 was limited, but the critic mistook a focused first release for the ceiling of the product.

author: davidu
cardQuote: I have a hard time seeing this replace specific purpose-driven tools (JIRA, Cerberus, etc.) even though it's gorgeous, functional, and has a cool off-line mode. It's just too generic for me.
quote:
My tweet is actually all I have to say about it: https://twitter.com/#!/davidu/status/131738215227981825 

 "Asana is beautifully designed. Seems too generic for bug, applicant or project tracking but it's going to be my new To-Do list manager." 

But to expand a bit -- I have a hard time seeing this replace specific purpose-driven tools (JIRA, Cerberus, etc.) even though it's gorgeous, functional, and has a cool off-line mode. It's just too generic for me. But for people who aren't coming from one of those products and have nothing today, it's a great way to introduce productivity. I'm surprised they didn't build in an SSO / LDAP kind of integration...

Finally - Salesforce focused on CRM as a use-case before branching out and getting less specific (support, chatter, etc.). Starting out generic requires your users to figure out how to apply it to their life, which I think is the wrong strategy.
storyTitle: Introducing Asana: The Modern Way to Work Together
outcome: Asana went public in 2020 at a valuation above $4B and remains a major work-management platform.
outcomeDetail: Asana direct-listed on the NYSE in September 2020 and was valued at more than $4 billion on its first day. It continues to sell team and enterprise work-management software.
note: The "too generic" critique missed that a flexible task tool could win teams that did not want a specialized bug tracker.

author: ryanwaggoner
cardQuote: 10% is really steep to me. That's just going to heavily incentivize your most successful users to bail.
quote:
Looks interesting, but 10% is really steep to me.

That’s just going to heavily incentivize your most successful users to bail. I run a five figure paid email service and I’m using a membership management service that charges flat fee plus 2%, and it annoys me every month. I’ll be replacing them this year. Membership billing plus a synced email list on Mailchimp is really commodity at this point. Doesn’t make any sense to pay a percentage of revenue.

If it was 10%, I’d replace them this week.

I may get pushback because there’s a contingent of people on here who basically seem to think that ever worrying about price for software and services is the wrong move. I think that’s pretty stupid when you’re a small company. It’s stupidly easy for a lot of small companies who are paying hundreds or thousands per month in recurring subscriptions to shave 20-30% off. If you’re a solo founder, that’s a huge increase in your personal bottom line.

EDIT: I'm probably coming across as too negative here, so let me add a few thoughts:

1. You built something useful, launched it, and have paying customers. That's HUGE and puts you ahead of 99% of "startups" so congrats :)

2. I strongly believe in the power of paid publishing and email marketing (it drives almost 100% of my income these days), and I think more cool tools and platforms in this space is excellent. This is the kind of thing that I would use.

My only real issue is just that I think what you're doing with the pricing model is shooting yourself in the foot (since it incentivizes people to switch away) AND it's unfair to users (since switching away is REALLY hard, and you probably know that and are counting on it to some extent).

Maybe charge flat + fee up to a cap? It'd be really comforting to know that I'd never pay more than $495 / month for this or something, and that would only be once I hit $10k / month in revenue or whatever.
storyTitle: Launch HN: Substack (YC W18): Paid email newsletters made simple
outcome: Substack kept its 10% cut and grew past 500,000 paying subscribers by late 2021.
outcomeDetail: Substack's revenue share remained central to its model as the platform scaled. By November 2021 it reported more than 500,000 paying subscribers and over one million paid subscriptions.
note: The churn prediction was reasonable, but Substack's writers stayed because the platform brought them readers and billing they did not have to build.

author: jimminy
cardQuote: people would begin to avoid them, reducing their effectiveness as a possible sales medium. Without oversight, as to who is selling a link, this might end up smothering itself out.
quote:
First off, I like the idea, but there are some noticeable flaws, many which have been brought up.

One interesting one for me, which is more an oversight, is that anyone can make money off of the sale of a link. There is no way to validate that the person posting the link, is the owner of the content. So someone could sell links to a page on HN, Reddit, Techcrunch, etc. at no expense to them.

If this did occur, I think it would cause a quite negative view of Gumroad links, as being scammy. In which case, people would begin to avoid them, reducing their effectiveness as a possible sales medium. Without oversight, as to who is selling a link, this might end up smothering itself out.
storyTitle: Show HN: my weekend project, Gumroad
outcome: Gumroad remains an independent creator-commerce platform, with creators earning about $2M in a recent week.
outcomeDetail: Gumroad survived its early trust and fraud problems and stayed independent rather than following a conventional venture path. In 2026 its site reported roughly $2 million in creator sales in a single week, and it remains a common way to sell digital products.
note: The scam-link fear was real, but Gumroad's fraud controls and simple checkout kept it useful; the marketplace never smothered itself.

author: evgen
cardQuote: the long periods of stagnation in releases eventually pushed me elsewhere... once I leave I am probably never going to come back.
quote: Add one more to the 'this should have been out two years ago' crowd. Early Things user (mostly via the iOS apps), stuck around through one long wait cycle for a major rev, but the long periods of stagnation in releases eventually pushed me elsewhere. GTD/productivity systems like this are very sticky. Once I commit and spend the time moving to a system I am unlikely to move to another, but once I leave I am probably never going to come back. Too bad, because when it first came out Things was a major improvement to the hacked-together options people were using at the time, but the more I look back on my time with Things the more convinced I am that they should have spent less time aiming for perfect and more time GTD.
storyTitle: “Things 3” Released
outcome: Things 3 won a 2017 Apple Design Award and Cultured Code still sells it across Apple platforms.
outcomeDetail: Cultured Code released Things 3 in May 2017 and won an Apple Design Award later that year. The app remains a flagship paid task manager for macOS, iOS, iPadOS, and visionOS.
note: The critic had already moved on, but the long-awaited release revived the product for new users and won Apple's design award.

storyTitle: Introducing Quip
outcome: Salesforce acquired Quip for a reported $750M in 2016; the product was retired a decade later.
outcomeDetail: Quip built an enterprise customer base and Salesforce bought it in 2016 for an estimated $750 million. It never became a category leader, and in March 2026 Salesforce announced that Quip would be retired, with subscriptions non-renewable after March 2027.
note: The critic was right that Quip would not displace Word, but wrong to imply the business world would not buy it. Salesforce paid $750M for the company and kept the product alive for another decade.
